edges.description: Loss of descending corticospinal input produces spastic weakness of the legs, with the extra-corticospinal features of the complicated form.
Corticospinal upper motor neuron tract degeneration above the lumbar cord causes upper- and lower-limb hyperreflexia.

Accompanying upper motor neuron corticobulbar projection involvement (closely paralleling descending corticospinal pyramidal tract degeneration rather than spinal corticospinal fibers themselves) manifests clinically as pseudobulbar dysarthria and dysphagia.
Loss and thinning of interhemispheric callosal fibers manifests directly on brain MRI as a thin corpus callosum.

edges.description: Axonal degeneration of peripheral motor and sensory fibers manifests clinically and electrodiagnostically as peripheral neuropathy.
Progressive lower-limb spasticity and paraparesis form the defining motor manifestation.
Progressive spastic paraparesis leads to wheelchair dependence within one to two decades of symptom onset in most patients.
Pes cavus foot deformity occurs as a less frequent musculoskeletal complication of chronic motor involvement in SPG11.
Scoliosis occurs as a less frequent musculoskeletal complication of chronic neuromuscular involvement in SPG11.

nodes.description: Impaired autolysosomal clearance leaves undegraded material and unexported lysosomal lipids inside neurons. In spatacsin-knockout mice the degenerating neurons accumulate autofluorescent material that stains for the lysosomal protein Lamp1 and for p62, the marker of substrate destined for autophagic degradation, lipidated LC3 is raised, and lipid clearance from lysosomes is perturbed. The burden falls on particularly sensitive neurons, including cortical motor neurons, cerebellar Purkinje cells, hippocampal neurons, and spinal motor neurons in knockout mice, corresponding to the central and peripheral features of the human disease.

evidence.reference_title: In Vivo Evidence for Lysosome Depletion and Impaired Autophagic Clearance in Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia Type SPG11.
evidence.snippet: Because lysosomes are reduced in cortical neurons and Purkinje cells in vivo, we propose that the decreased number of lysosomes available for fusion with autophagosomes impairs autolysosomal clearance, results in the accumulation of undegraded material and finally causes death of particularly sensitive neurons like cortical motoneurons and Purkinje cells in knockout mice.

nodes.description: Loss of spatacsin depletes the pool of free lysosomes that are competent to fuse with incoming autophagosomes, while autolysosomes accumulate - the signature of a blocked reformation step rather than a blocked degradation step. Lysosomal function per se is largely preserved: cathepsin D processing and lysosomal pH are normal in spatacsin-null cells, and what is reduced is the number of lysosomes, not their competence. The distinction matters, because it makes SPG11 a disorder of lysosome supply rather than a classical lysosomal storage disease.

nodes.description: The clinical endpoint: progressive spasticity and weakness of the lower limbs with onset mainly in infancy or adolescence, though the reported range runs from age 1 to 31 years and rarely as late as 60. Most affected individuals become wheelchair bound one or two decades after onset. SPG11 is a complicated rather than a pure HSP, so the paraparesis is accompanied by cognitive impairment, peripheral neuropathy, pseudobulbar involvement, and upper-limb hyperreflexia, with cerebellar signs, retinal degeneration, and parkinsonism as less frequent additions.

evidence.snippet: Spastic paraplegia 11 (SPG11) is characterized by progressive spasticity and weakness of the lower limbs frequently associated with the following: mild intellectual disability with learning difficulties in childhood and/or progressive cognitive decline; peripheral neuropathy; pseudobulbar involvement; and increased reflexes in the upper limbs.

Onset occurs mainly during infancy or adolescence (range: age 1-31 years) and in rare cases as late as age 60 years. Most affected individuals become wheelchair bound one or two decades after disease onset.

nodes.description: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in SPG11 abolish spatacsin. Spatacsin is an essential component of autophagic lysosome reformation, the pathway that regenerates free lysosomes out of autolysosomes once autophagic degradation is complete, and it acts in the same step as spastizin, the product of the other common autosomal recessive HSP gene SPG15. Both proteins are required for the initiation of the lysosomal tubulation that pinches off new lysosomes. This places SPG11 in the endolysosomal and membrane-traffic category of HSP genes, alongside the AP-4 and AP-5 complex disorders.

evidence.reference_title: Spastic paraplegia proteins spastizin and spatacsin mediate autophagic lysosome reformation.
evidence.snippet: Here, we have demonstrated that the two most common autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia gene products, the SPG15 protein spastizin and the SPG11 protein spatacsin, are pivotal for autophagic lysosome reformation (ALR), a pathway that generates new lysosomes.
